lead: A particle changes velocity only because forces act on it, and Newton's second law states that exactly: ΣF = ma. In an inertial frame this vector equation, split into components, answers every acceleration question for machines and vehicles. D'Alembert's principle adds a fictitious inertia force −ma and turns the same problem into statics. This chapter covers the free body diagram, three component forms and the dynamic-equilibrium trick, then works a crate on a rough floor.
prereq: You need: free body diagrams and resolution of forces (Unit 1), the laws of friction and μk (Unit 3), and the acceleration components in 5.2.

sections.h3: The second law and what an inertial frame means

blocks.text: Newton's second law for a particle says the net force on it equals its mass times its acceleration.

blocks.where: ΣF is the vector sum of every real force on the particle, in N; m is its mass in kg; a is its acceleration in m/s², measured in an inertial frame. The equation is a vector equation, so it holds separately along every chosen direction.

blocks.text: An inertial frame does not itself accelerate. The ground is close enough for a trolley on a factory floor. A braking bus is not inertial: a book on its floor slides forward with no horizontal force, so ΣF = 0 while a ≠ 0 and the law fails. In an accelerating frame add a pseudo-force −mA, where A is the frame's acceleration.
The law as written is for one particle: a body whose parts do not move relative to each other, or one whose rotation you can ignore.

items: Draw the free body diagram: weight mg, normals N, tensions T, friction f, applied forces, and nothing else.
Choose axes so that the acceleration has as few components as possible.
Write ΣF = ma along each axis, fixing the positive sense in advance.
Solve the unknowns. Find each normal reaction before you use friction.
Check that a points the same way as the net force, and that units are N, kg, m/s² only.

sections.h3: The law in three component systems

blocks.text: Rectangular axes (x, y, z) fit forces with fixed directions: weight down, normal perpendicular to the floor, a rope at a stated angle, friction along the surface.
ΣF<sub>x</sub> = m a<sub>x</sub>,  ΣF<sub>y</sub> = m a<sub>y</sub>,  ΣF<sub>z</sub> = m a<sub>z</sub>
blocks.where: ΣF<sub>x</sub> is the sum of x-components of all forces in N; a<sub>x</sub> is the x-component of acceleration in m/s², and likewise for y and z.

blocks.text: Normal-tangential axes (t, n) fit a particle whose path is known. Take t along the tangent, in the direction of motion, and n along the principal normal, pointing to the centre of curvature.
ΣF<sub>t</sub> = m a<sub>t</sub> = m dv/dt,  ΣF<sub>n</sub> = m a<sub>n</sub> = m v²/ρ
blocks.where: v is the speed in m/s, ρ is the radius of curvature in m, a<sub>t</sub> changes the speed and a<sub>n</sub> changes the direction. The n-equation demands a force even when the speed is constant, as for a car on a bend.

blocks.text: Cylindrical axes (r, θ, z) fit a particle on a rotating arm or a slider on a rotating rod: write ΣFr = m ar, ΣFθ = m aθ, ΣFz = m az, taking ar and aθ from the chapter on cylindrical components.

On a rough surface friction is one more force in ΣF: get N from the equation perpendicular to sliding, then put f = μ<sub>k</sub>N opposite to the sliding velocity, where μ<sub>k</sub> is the coefficient of kinetic friction. Never assume N = mg; use the perpendicular equation.
Move the right side of the second law to the left.
ΣF − m a = 0,  that is  Σ(F − m a) = 0
blocks.where: −m a is the inertia force: magnitude m a in N, direction opposite to the acceleration. Nothing physically pushes with it; it is a bookkeeping device.

blocks.text: With the inertia force added, the forces sum to zero, the body is in dynamic equilibrium, and every tool of statics applies unchanged. Moments balance too: ΣM<sub>O</sub> of the real forces plus the moment of −m a about O is zero, which lets you take moments about a point to kill unknown reactions. A lift cage or bracket becomes a statics problem. For the particle of this chapter the single inertia force is enough. A rigid body that spins as well also needs the inertia couple of magnitude I<sub>G</sub>α opposite to the angular acceleration, where I<sub>G</sub> is the mass moment of inertia about the centre of mass in kg·m² and α the angular acceleration in rad/s².

items: Never mix the two forms in one problem. Either draw the real free body diagram and write ΣF = m a, or add −m a and write ΣF = 0. Doing both counts m a twice.
The inertia force acts through the centre of mass, so its moment arm is measured from there.
The principle changes nothing physical; it only changes which set of equations you write.

blocks.text: Systems of particles. Sum the equation over all particles; internal forces cancel in pairs and only external forces survive.

blocks.where: ΣF<sub>ext</sub> is the sum of external forces in N, M the total mass in kg, and a<sub>cm</sub> the acceleration of the centre of mass in m/s². A cricket bat flung into the air spins wildly, yet its centre of mass follows the simple parabola of a single particle of mass M.

figure.caption: The route from crate to answer: free body diagram, vertical equation for N, then friction, then horizontal equation for a. The 30° pull lowers N below the weight.

spec.title: Crate pulled at 30°
spec.aria: The chain from the crate to the answer: draw the free body diagram, use vertical equilibrium to get the normal force, apply Newton's second law horizontally, and read off the acceleration.

examples.question: A 50 kg crate rests on a horizontal floor. A rope pulls it with tension T = 200 N at 30° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between crate and floor is μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.25 and g = 9.81 m/s². The crate slides. Find its acceleration.
steps: Tension components: T cos30° = 200 × 0.8660 = 173.2 N horizontal; T sin30° = 200 × 0.5000 = 100.0 N vertical, upwards.
Vertical direction: the crate does not leave the floor, so a<sub>y</sub> = 0. ΣF<sub>y</sub> = N + T sin30° − mg = 0, hence N = 490.5 − 100.0 = 390.5 N.
Friction, opposing the sliding: f = μ<sub>k</sub>N = 0.25 × 390.5 = 97.6 N.
Horizontal direction: ΣF<sub>x</sub> = T cos30° − f = 173.2 − 97.6 = 75.6 N.
Second law: a = ΣF<sub>x</sub>/m = 75.6/50 = 1.51 m/s², along the floor in the direction of the pull.
D'Alembert check: add an inertia force of 50 × 1.512 = 75.6 N backwards (about 75.5 N if you keep a = 1.51 m/s²); then 173.2 = 97.6 + 75.6, so the forces balance.
examples.answer: The crate accelerates at 1.51 m/s² along the floor, in the direction of the pull.
examples.check:
import math
m = 50.0
T = 200.0
th = math.radians(30.0)
g = 9.81
mu = 0.25
N = m*g - T*math.sin(th)
f = mu*N
tx = T*math.cos(th)
net = tx - f
a = net/m
print(round(N, 1))
print(round(f, 1))
print(round(tx, 1))
print(round(net, 1))
print(round(a, 2))

traps: Writing ΣF = m a while the inertia force is also drawn on the diagram. That counts m a twice: the net real force is shared between two m a terms, so you report half the true acceleration. Choose one form and stay with it.
Putting N = mg when the rope is inclined. An upward pull at angle θ gives N = mg − T sinθ, smaller than mg, so friction μ<sub>k</sub>N drops as well; a downward push raises N and raises friction.
Applying ΣF = m a inside an accelerating lift, train or trolley without the pseudo-force −mA for that frame.
On a curved path, forgetting the normal equation. Even at constant speed a<sub>n</sub> = v²/ρ needs its own force, so the net force is not along the tangent.
Feeding a tension given in kgf straight into ΣF = m a. Multiply by 9.81 to get newtons first.

quiz.q: State Newton's second law for a particle and name the frame in which it holds.
quiz.a: ΣF = m a: the net force in N equals mass in kg times acceleration in m/s². It holds in an inertial (non-accelerating) frame.
A frame that does not itself accelerate. The ground is a good approximation for short, slow motions; an accelerating bus is not inertial.

quiz.q: Why does D'Alembert's principle let you solve a dynamics problem with statics?
quiz.a: Adding the inertia force −m a makes the vector sum of all forces zero, Σ(F − m a) = 0. Equilibrium conditions, including ΣM = 0 about any point, then hold for the real forces plus the inertia force, so statics methods apply directly.

quiz.q: A 20 kg block slides on a rough horizontal floor under a horizontal pull of 100 N. μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.3, g = 9.81 m/s². Find the acceleration.
A 60 kg person stands on a lift floor that accelerates upwards at 2 m/s². Find the floor reaction on the person, with g = 9.81 m/s².
quiz.a: N − mg = ma gives N = m(g + a) = 60 × (9.81 + 2) = 708.6 N upwards. With the inertia force drawn downwards, N = mg + ma balances.

quiz.q: The same crate is pulled with the same tension but at 30° above the horizontal instead of horizontally. Explain the two opposite effects on the acceleration.
quiz.a: The horizontal drive falls from T to T cos30° = 0.866T, which lowers the acceleration. At the same time the normal reaction falls to mg − T sin30°, so friction μ<sub>k</sub>N falls too, which raises it. The net result depends on μ<sub>k</sub>; here the drive loss dominates at μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.25.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car rounds a flat circular curve of radius 50 m at a steady 20 m/s. Which equation supplies the sideways force, and how large is it?
quiz.a: The normal equation ΣF<sub>n</sub> = m a<sub>n</sub> = m v²/ρ. Here a<sub>n</sub> = 400/50 = 8 m/s², so the friction on the tyres must be 1000 × 8 = 8000 N, directed towards the centre of the curve.

beyond: Not for the exam. Adding −m a to every particle and summing is how Lagrange's equations are derived from D'Alembert's principle, and the same step becomes virtual work for dynamic systems. Multibody software such as ADAMS, Simscape or MuJoCo assembles ΣF − m a = 0 for thousands of bodies and solves it numerically at each time step. Vehicle rollover limits, robot arm sizing and shake-table testing of brackets all start from a free body diagram plus an inertia force.
